title: Saint Francis (4 October)
hook: the day animals are brought to church for blessing
tomorrow: Our Lady of the Rosary (7 October)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Our Lady of Sorrows and the poem Stabat Mater. Your line was the mother stood. Who did you stay with a little longer? Day six hundred eighty-three.

On or near the fourth of October, parish parking lots fill up with dogs on leashes, cats in carriers, a hamster in a shoebox, sometimes a horse, a goat, a goldfish in a bowl, and once in a while a very patient iguana. A priest walks down the line with holy water and blesses each one. It's noisy and a little chaotic, and people who haven't been to church in years show up. The man behind it all died centuries ago, and near the end of his life, nearly blind and in pain, he wrote a song.
screen: `DOGS, CATS, A GOLDFISH.` → `A BLESSING FOR EACH ONE.` → `A SONG FROM A SICKBED.`

segments.voice: Francis of Assisi was the son of a rich cloth merchant. He wanted to be a knight. Instead, after illness and a stint as a prisoner of war, he gave it all up, stripping off even his clothes before the bishop and his father, and lived in poverty, rebuilding ruined churches, caring for lepers, preaching peace. Others came to share that life, and then more. The stories about animals are famous: preaching to the birds, making peace with a wolf that terrified the town of Gubbio. Those come from collections written after his death, and people tell them as stories. But the song is his own. Near the end of his life, sick and almost blind, staying at San Damiano, he wrote the Canticle of the Creatures, not in Latin but in the everyday Italian of Umbria. It begins Laudato si', mi' Signore, praised be you, my Lord, and then it praises God through creation, calling each part family: brother sun, who brings the day; sister moon and the stars; brother wind; sister water, useful and humble and precious and pure; brother fire; and our sister, mother earth. Near his death he added one more verse, for sister death. The idea is older than Francis. The Book of Daniel, in the Catholic Bible, has three young men in a furnace singing, in the Douay-Rheims: "All ye works of the Lord, bless the Lord." What Francis added was the family. Not resources. Not scenery. Kin. In 2015 a pope who took his name borrowed the first line for a letter on care for the earth.
screen: `A RICH MAN'S SON GIVES IT ALL UP.` · `BIRDS AND A WOLF: STORIES TOLD.` · `THE CANTICLE OF THE CREATURES.` · `BROTHER SUN, SISTER WATER.` · then, large: `ALL YE WORKS OF THE LORD, BLESS THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless an animal. If you have a pet, sit beside it and rest a hand on it. If you don't, find an animal you can see: a bird at the window, a dog across the street, even an ant on the sidewalk, or picture one you've loved. Watch it breathe. Notice that it's alive, the way you are. If you pray, you can ask God to bless it. If you don't, wish it well, as kin. The bell holds the time.
Saint Francis. Francis of Assisi, the poor man who called the sun his brother and the earth his sister. His feast is the fourth of October. Today's word.
Your line: brother sun. Today, when you step into sunlight, greet it the way Francis did, as family, even silently. Day six hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Francis of Assisi on 4 October, and many parishes hold a blessing of animals on or near the day; Franciscans celebrate it as a solemnity.

fork.setup: you're Francis near the end of your life: sick, nearly blind, in pain, staying at San Damiano. what do you write?
options: a letter of complaint about your treatment.
a song praising God through brother sun and sister water.
fork.reveal: he wrote the Canticle of the Creatures, calling the sun, moon, wind, water, fire and earth his family.

original.note: Umbrian Italian, a daughter of Latin: brother sun, from the Canticle of the Creatures.

trapdoor: what you thought: the saint who liked animals.
what it means: a rich man's son who chose poverty and called all creation his family.
what a scholar hears: a Canticle in Umbrian, not Latin, echoing Daniel's song of the three young men.

notes: Prisoner of war after the battle of Collestrada (1202); confirm.
Canticle composed 1225 at San Damiano; 'sister death' verse added shortly before his death in October 1226; confirm.
The canticle's opening 'Laudato si', mi' Signore' is given in the voice as a phrase, not cited as a quotation; the creature list is the writer's paraphrase.
Daniel 3:57 in the Douay-Rheims (deuterocanonical part of Daniel 3); confirm wording.
